`..` is a literal hard link that is created for every directory that points to the parent directory, of which there only is of course only one. It seems consistent from that point of view that it should be treated as any other file and `ln -s somewhere/whatever symlink ; cd symlink ; cd ..` should resolve to `somewhere` which is the parent directory of the directory pointed at by `symlink`.

However, in UNIX, what is actually "correct" is mandated by POSIX, and POSIX, not necessarily consistent, mandates that the `cd` command should resolve `..` *logically* unless the `-P` option is specified. If the `-P` option is specified, it should however resolve symbolic links before attempting to change the directory and reset `PWD`, just as you prefer.

So what `cd argument` actually does when the `-P` flag is not specified is to take the current `PWD`, append the argument to it and then symbolically resolve every `..` component and make sure that the resulting path resolves to a directory, call `chdir` with that path and also reset `PWD` to that path. That is, if the result of the concatenation is `a/b/c/../d`, it mangles the string into `a/b/d` without any regard for what `c` is or where it physically resides, and that'll be your new `PWD` and as such the basis for any further `cd` invocation. It's literally just mangling the string without any regard for what anything represents physically.

So you're now seeing Fish improving its POSIX compliance. If you prefer that symlinks are resolved, use the -P option.

EDIT: Here's the spec: https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/009695399/utilities/cd.html. > Say you bought a vintage computer and wanted to code a graphical game could that be done? 

Yes, the machine was essentially made for that purpose and thousands of graphical games exist for it.

> Like I want to buy a vintage computer and learn to make programs and graphics and stuff on the system just for fun where do I start?

When you boot the machine you end up in a line-oriented BASIC editor. From here you can write BASIC programs. BASIC is a simple language, and the manual for it was bundled with the machine. It's slow, but a good place to start learning some of the hardware, because you can directly access the peripheral hardware registers from it. The manual contains some programs for playing music and displaying sprites.

Most commercial games were distributed as machine language binaries. The computer has a 6502 compatible CPU. This was a very popular CPU at the time, so there are a lot of resources on how to program it online. The instruction set is very simple which on one hand means that it is easy to learn its instruction set, but also means that you have to implement things like multiplication manually. The benefit is that this is typically orders of magnitude faster than BASIC code.

Machine language programs are typically *assembled* from instruction mnemonics. The assembler turns these mnemonics into the corresponding machine operations and handles other things like macros and named memory addresses. For this computer I use the Acme assembler which can be run on a modern system. There is another assembler called KickAssembler which I think would be good for a beginner because of its extensive manual and macro library.

The hardware peripherals like the graphics and sound chips are operated through memory mapped registers and shared memory. For example, the text on the screen when you boot the machine resides in 1000 (40 * 25) bytes of memory location 1024 to 2024. There is a popular book that describes what all the memory in the machine is used for called "Mapping the Computer". A computer version is available here: http://unusedino.de/ec64/technical/project64/mapping_c64.html. In BASIC, you can try manipulating it with e.g. `POKE 1024,0`, which should display an "@" in the first row of the first column of the text area.

http://codebase64.org covers a lot of different topics from beginner stuff to advanced tricks, but I'd recommend starting with BASIC to see where that takes you.
